claim: The ability to calibrate learning according to new information is a fundamental component of an organism's ability to adapt to changing conditions.
source: The ability to calibrate learning according to new information is a fundamental component of an organism's ability to adapt to changing conditions.
evidence: This is a general statement about adaptive learning that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: The exact neural mechanisms guiding dynamic learning rate adjustments remain unclear.
source: Yet, the exact neural mechanisms guiding dynamic learning rate adjustments remain unclear.
evidence: This statement acknowledges a gap in current scientific knowledge.

claim: Catecholamines appear to play a critical role in adjusting the degree to which we use new information over time.
source: Catecholamines appear to play a critical role in adjusting the degree to which we use new information over time, but individuals vary widely in the manner in which they adjust to changes.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to existing literature on catecholamines and learning.

claim: Individuals vary widely in the manner in which they adjust to changes.
source: Catecholamines appear to play a critical role in adjusting the degree to which we use new information over time, but individuals vary widely in the manner in which they adjust to changes.
evidence: This is a general observation about individual differences in learning.

claim: Participants completed a reversal learning task during a drug-free baseline session.
source: Participants first completed a reversal learning task during a drug-free baseline session to provide a measure of baseline performance.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: Participants completed the task during two sessions, one with MA (20 mg oral) and one with placebo.
source: Then they completed the task during two sessions, one with MA (20 mg oral) and one with placebo (PL).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: Relative to placebo, methamphetamine modulates the ability to dynamically adjust learning from prediction errors.
source: First, we showed that, relative to PL, MA modulates the ability to dynamically adjust learning from prediction errors.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: The effect of methamphetamine on learning was more pronounced in participants who performed moderately low at baseline.
source: Second, this effect was more pronounced in participants who performed moderately low at baseline.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Baseline performance modulates the effect of methamphetamine.
source: These results present novel evidence for the involvement of catecholaminergic transmission on learning flexibility and highlights that baseline performance modulates the effect of the drug.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Humans are able to calibrate learning rates according to the statistical content of new information.
source: A burgeoning literature suggests that humans are able to calibrate learning rates according to the statistical content of new information (Behrens et al., 2007; Cook et al., 2019; Diederen et al., 2016; Nassar et al., 2019; Nassar et al., 2010; Razmi and Nassar, 2022), albeit to varying degrees (Kirschner et al., 2022; Kirschner et al., 2024; Nassar et al., 2016; Nassar et al., 2012; Nassar et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Optimal learning requires increased weighting of surprising information during periods of change and ignoring surprising events during periods of stability.
source: In environments that include discontinuities (changepoints) and noise (probabilistic errors), optimal learning requires increased weighting of surprising information during periods of change and ignoring surprising events during periods of stability.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about optimal learning strategies.

claim: Striatal dopaminergic prediction errors act as a teaching signal in cortico–striatal circuits to learn task structure and rules.
source: For example, a class of models assumes that striatal dopaminergic prediction errors act as a teaching signal in cortico–striatal circuits to learn task structure and rules (Badre and Frank, 2012; Collins and Frank, 2013; Collins and Frank, 2016; Lieder et al., 2018; Pasupathy and Miller, 2005; Schultz et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to computational models in the literature.

claim: Dopamine plays a role in tracking the reward history with multiple learning rates.
source: Another line of research highlights the role of dopamine in tracking the reward history with multiple learning rates (Doya, 2002; Kolling et al., 2016; Meder et al., 2017; Schweighofer and Doya, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Dopamine in the prefrontal cortex and basal ganglia is involved in modulating computational tradeoffs such as cognitive stability–flexibility balance.
source: Within the broader literature of cognitive control, it has been suggested that dopamine in the prefrontal cortex and basal ganglia is involved in modulating computational tradeoffs such as cognitive stability–flexibility balance (Cools, 2008; Dreisbach et al., 2005; Floresco, 2013; Goschke, 2013; Goschke and Bolte, 2014; Goschke and Bolte, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The locus coeruleus/norepinephrine system is important in facilitating adaptive learning and structure learning.
source: Finally, other theories highlight the importance of the locus coeruleus/norepinephrine system in facilitating adaptive learning and structure learning (Razmi and Nassar, 2022; Silvetti et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Catecholaminergic drugs are known to affect cognitive performance including probabilistic reversal learning.
source: Consistent with these neuro-computational models catecholaminergic drugs are known to affect cognitive performance including probabilistic reversal learning (Cook et al., 2019; Dodds et al., 2008; Repantis et al., 2010; Rostami Kandroodi et al., 2021; van den Bosch et al., 2022; Westbrook et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Psychostimulants that increase extracellular catecholamine availability can enhance cognition.
source: Indeed, psychostimulants, such as methamphetamine (MA), that increase extracellular catecholamine availability, can enhance cognition (Arria et al., 2017; Husain and Mehta, 2011; Smith and Farah, 2011) and are used to remediate cognitive deficits in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (Arnsten and Pliszka, 2011; Prince, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The cognitive enhancements from psychostimulants vary across tasks and across individuals.
source: However, the cognitive enhancements vary across tasks and across individuals (Bowman et al., 2023; Cook et al., 2019; Cools and D'Esposito, 2011; Garrett et al., 2015; Rostami Kandroodi et al., 2021; van den Bosch et al., 2022; van der Schaaf et al., 2013) and the mechanisms underlying this variability remain poorly understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The effects of catecholaminergic drugs depend on an individual's baseline dopamine levels in the prefrontal cortex and striatum.
source: There is evidence that the effects of catecholaminergic drugs depend on an individual's baseline dopamine levels in the prefrontal cortex and striatum (Cohen and Servan-Schreiber, 1992; Cools and D'Esposito, 2011; Dodds et al., 2008; Durstewitz and Seamans, 2008; Rostami Kandroodi et al., 2021; van den Bosch et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Pushing dopamine from low to optimal levels may increase update thresholds in the light of new information.
source: For example, pushing dopamine from low to optimal (medium) levels may increase update thresholds in the light of new information (i.e., facilitating shielding/stability), whereas if a drug pushes dopamine either too high or too low may decrease update thresholds (i.e., facilitating shifting/flexibility) (Durstewitz and Seamans, 2008; Goschke and Bolte, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical models.

claim: Methylphenidate did not alter reversal learning overall, but preferentially improved performance in participants with higher working memory capacity.
source: For example, Rostami Kandroodi et al., 2021 reported that the re-uptake blocker methylphenidate did not alter reversal learning overall, but preferentially improved performance in participants with higher working memory capacity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Ninety-four healthy young adults completed the probabilistic learning task on three separate sessions.
source: Ninety-four healthy young adults completed the probabilistic learning task (Figure 2; Fischer and Ullsperger, 2013; Jocham et al., 2014; Kirschner et al., 2022; Kirschner et al., 2024) on three separate sessions, an initial drug-free session, and after PL and MA.
evidence: This describes the study sample and design.

claim: The study followed a double-blinded cross-over design, whereby 50% of participants received MA first, and 50% of participants PL first.
source: The study followed a double-blinded cross-over design, whereby 50% of participants received MA first, and 50% of participants PL first.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The groups did not differ significantly on any of the demographic variables measured.
source: The groups did not differ significantly on any of the variables measured.
evidence: This is a result from statistical comparison of demographic data.

claim: There was a strong practice effect with better performance on session two and three compared to session one.
source: We found a strong practice effect (F(2,186) = 14.53, p < 0.001) with better performance on session two and three compared to session one (baseline).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: There was no difference in the total scores between session two and three.
source: There was no difference in the total scores between session two and three (see Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: MA administration significantly increased 'feel drug effect' ratings compared to PL at 30, 50, 135, 180, and 210 min post-capsule administration.
source: MA administration significantly increased 'feel drug effect' ratings compared to PL, at 30, 50, 135, 180, and 210 min post-capsule administration (see Figure 1; Drug × Time interaction F(5,555) = 38.46, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis with reference to Figure 1.

claim: In the MA session, no differences in the 'feel drug effect' were observed between low and high baseline performers.
source: In the MA session, no differences in the 'feel drug effect' were observed between low and high baseline performer, including peak change-from-baseline ratings (rating at 50 min post-capsule: low baseline performer: 48.36 (4.29) vs. high baseline performer: 47.21 (4.44); t(91) = 0.18, p = 0.85, d = 0.03; rating at 135 min post-capsule: low baseline performer: 37.27 (4.15) vs. high baseline performer: 45.38 (3.84); t(91) = 1.42, p = 0.15, d = 0.29).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Participants learned the task well, based on the observation that their choice behavior largely followed the underlying reward probabilities of the stimuli across the sessions.
source: In general, participants learned the task well, based on the observation that their choice behavior largely followed the underlying reward probabilities of the stimuli across the sessions (see Figure 4D-F).
evidence: This is an observation from the data with reference to Figure 4D-F.

claim: When all subjects were considered together, there was no performance benefit under MA quantified by the total points scored in the task.
source: When all subjects were considered together, we did not find a performance benefit under MA quantified by the total points scored in the task (MA: 736.59 (37.11) vs. PL: 702.02 (38.305); t(93) = 1.38, p = 0.17, d = 0.10).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: When participants were stratified by their baseline performance, there was a marginally significant Drug × Baseline Performance Group interaction.
source: When participants were stratified by their baseline performance (median spilt on total points at baseline), we found a marginally significant Drug × Baseline Performance Group interaction (Drug × Baseline Performance Group interaction: F(1,92) = 3.20, p = 0.07; see Figure 2C and 7A).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis with reference to figures.

claim: Compared to PL, MA improved performance marginally in participants with poor baseline performance.
source: Post hoc t-tests revealed that compared to PL, MA improved performance marginally in participants with poor baseline performance (total points MA: 522.55 (53.79) vs. PL: 443.61 (47.81); t(46) = 1.85, p = 0.071, d = 0.23).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc analysis.

claim: MA did not improve performance in the high baseline performance group.
source: MA did not, however, improve performance in the high baseline performance group (total points MA: 950.63 (26.15) vs. PL: 960.42 (27.26); t(46) = –0.38, p = 0.698, d = 0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc analysis.

claim: There was a trend for slightly faster RTs under MA.
source: There was a trend for slightly faster RTs under MA (PL: 544.67 ms (9.87) vs. MA: 533.84 ms (11.51); t(93) = 1.75, p = 0.08, d = 0.10).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: MA was associated with reduced RT variability.
source: Moreover, MA was associated with reduced RT variability (average individual SD of RTs: PL: 193.74 (6.44) vs. MA: 178.98 (5.47); t(93) = 2.54, p = 0.012, d = 0.25).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Reduced RT variability has previously been associated with increased attention and performance.
source: Reduced RT variability has previously been associated with increased attention and performance (Esterman et al., 2013; Karamacoska et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The MA-related reduction in RT variability was specific to low baseline performers.
source: Post hoc t-tests indicated that the MA-related reduction in RT variability was specific to low baseline performers (PL: 212.07 (9.84) vs. MA: 182.46 (7.98); t(46) = 3.04, p = 0.003, d = 0.48), whereas MA did not affect high baseline performers RT variability (PL: 175.40 (7.51) vs. MA: 175.50 (7.55); t(46) = –0.02, p = 0.98, d < 0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc analysis.

claim: The drug did not affect initial learning.
source: As shown in Figure 3, the drug did not affect initial learning.
evidence: This is an observation from the data with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The drug improved performance later in learning, particularly for stimuli with less predictable reward probabilities and in subjects with low baseline performance.
source: However, the drug improved performance later in learning, particularly for stimuli with less predictable reward probabilities (see Figure 3B) and in subjects with low baseline performance.
evidence: This is an observation from the data with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: One break point was identified at 10 trials after a reversal using the Bai–Perron multiple break point test.
source: One break point was identified at 10 trials after a reversal (indexed by the vertical lines in Figure 3).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis with reference to Figure 3.

claim: There was a trend for increased learning under MA for stimuli with less predictable rewards.
source: Interestingly, we found a trend for increased learning under MA for stimuli with less predictable rewards (PL: 0.80 (0.01) vs. 0.82 (0.01); t(93) = –1.80, p = 0.07, d = 0.14).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Subjects performing lower at baseline appeared to benefit from MA in late learning.
source: Post hoc t-tests revealed that subjects performing lower at baseline appeared to benefit from MA (average accuracy late learning PL: 0.69 (0.02) vs. MA: 0.74 (0.02); t(46) = –2.59, p = 0.01, d = 0.32), whereas there was no difference between MA and PL in the high baseline performance group (PL: 0.91 (0.01) vs. MA: 0.91 (0.01); t(46) = 0.29, p = 0.77, d = 0.04).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc analysis.

claim: The winning model was the Pearce–Hall hybrid feedback confirmatory model that allowed the learning rate to vary based on whether the feedback was confirmatory or not and the level of surprise of the outcome.
source: The winning model (as measured by lowest Bayesian information criterion [BIC] and achieving protected exceedance probabilities of 100%) was one that allowed the learning rate to vary based on whether the feedback was confirmatory or not and the level of surprise of the outcome (see Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a result from model comparison analysis with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: MA increases performance later in learning for stimuli with less predictable reward probabilities, particularly in subjects with low baseline performance, as shown by simulations.
source: Specifically, using individual maximum likelihood parameter estimates, we simulated task performance and confirmed that MA increases performance later in learning for stimuli with less predictable reward probabilities, particularly in subjects with low baseline performance (Figure 5A; mean ± SD: simPL low performance: 0.69 ± 0.01 vs. simMA low performance: 0.72 ± 0.01; t(46) = 2.00, p = 0.03, d = 0.23).
evidence: This is a result from simulation analysis with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: Eta (the parameter controlling dynamic adjustments of learning rate according to recent absolute prediction errors) was reduced under MA.
source: We found that eta (the parameter controlling dynamic adjustments of learning rate according to recent absolute prediction errors) was reduced under MA (eta MA: 0.24 (0.01) vs. PL: 0.30 (0.01); t(93) = –3.005, p = 0.003, d = 0.43).
evidence: This is a statistical result from model parameter comparison.

claim: Subjects performing less well at baseline showed smaller eta's under MA compared to PL.
source: Post hoc t tests revealed that compared to PL, MA affected eta depending on baseline performance in the task. Here, subjects performing less well at baseline showed smaller eta's (eta MA: 0.24 (0.01) vs. 0.33 (0.02); t(46) = –3.06, p = 0.003, d = 0.67), whereas there was no difference between MA and PL in the high baseline performance group MA: 0.23 (0.01) vs. 0.26 (0.01); t(46) = –1.03, p = 0.31, d = 0.18.
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc analysis.

claim: MA appears to be associated with reduced learning rate dynamics in low baseline performers.
source: As suggested by lower eta scores, MA appears to be associated with reduced learning rate dynamics in low baseline performers.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model parameter results.

claim: Low baseline performers in the PL condition exhibited greater variability in learning rate rendering their choices more erratic.
source: In contrast, low baseline performers in the PL condition exhibited greater variability in learning rate (and average LR throughout) rendering their choices more erratic.
evidence: This is an observation from the learning rate trajectory analysis.

claim: Variability in learning rate was reduced under MA in both early and late stages of learning across all reversals.
source: Specifically, variability in learning rate (average individual SD of learning rate) was reduced in both early and late stages of learning across all reversals (early PL: 0.20 (0.01) vs. MA: 0.17 (0.01); t(93) = 2.72, p = 0.007, d = 0.36; late PL: 0.18 (0.01) vs. MA: 0.15 (0.01); t(93) = 2.51, p = 0.01, d = 0.33), as were reversals to stimuli with less predictable rewards (early PL: 0.19 (0.01) vs. 0.16 (0.01); t(93) = 2.98, p = 0.003, d = 0.39; late PL: 0.18 (0.01) vs. MA: 0.16 (0.01); t(93) = 2.66, p = 0.009, d=0.35).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: People with high baseline performance show a large difference in learning rates after true reversals and during the rest of the task including misleading feedback.
source: Together, these patterns of results suggest that people with high baseline performance show a large difference in learning rates after true reversals and during the rest of the task including misleading feedback.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the learning rate trajectory analysis.

claim: High baseline performers show a peak in learning after reversals and reduced learning rates in later periods of a learning block, when choice preferences should ideally be stabilized.
source: Specifically, they show a peak in learning after reversals and reduced learning rates in later periods of a learning block, when choice preferences should ideally be stabilized (see Figure 6C).
evidence: This is an observation from the data with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: High baseline performers have a better signal-to-noise ratio between real reversals and misleading feedback.
source: This results in a better signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) between real reversals and misleading feedback (i.e., surprising outcomes in the late learning stage).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the learning rate trajectory analysis.

claim: In low baseline performers the SNR is improved after the administration of MA.
source: In low baseline performers the SNR is improved after the administration of MA.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the learning rate trajectory analysis.

claim: MA significantly increased the SNR for low baseline performers.
source: The results of this analysis revealed that MA significantly increased the SNR for low baseline performers (PL: 0.01 (0.01) vs. MA: 0.04 (0.01); t(46) = –2.81, p = 0.007, d = 0.49).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Higher eta scores were associated with fewer correct choices after two consecutive probabilistic errors.
source: We found a significant correlation across participants (see Figure 7), whereby higher etas scores were associated with fewer correct choices (r = 0.29, p = <0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis with reference to Figure 7.

claim: There was a trend toward a drug effect, with subjects in MA condition being more likely to make the correct choice after two misleading feedbacks.
source: There was a trend toward a drug effect, with subjects in MA condition being more likely to make the correct choice after two misleading feedbacks (PL: 0.82 (0.02) vs. 0.84 (0.01); t(93) = –1.92, p = 0.06, d = 0.13).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Low baseline performers showed higher correct choice probabilities under MA after two misleading feedbacks.
source: Post hoc t-tests indicated higher correct choice probabilities under MA in low baseline performers (PL: 0.70 (0.02) vs. MA: 0.75 (0.02); t(46) = –2.41, p = 0.02, d = 0.30) but not in high baseline performers (PL: 0.92 (0.01234) vs. MA: 0.92 (0.01); t(46) = 0.11, p = 0.91, d = 0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc analysis.

claim: Play bias and eta both made a significant negative contribution to overall task performance.
source: The results of this analysis revealed that variability in several of the parameters was related to overall task performance, with the overall learning rate, feedback confirmation LR adjustments, and inverse temperature all positively predicting performance and eta and the play bias term negatively predicting it.
evidence: This is a result from regression analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Only the parameter controlling dynamic adjustments of learning rate according to recent prediction errors, eta, was affected by the pharmacological manipulation.
source: While each of these parameters explained unique variance in overall performance levels, only the parameter controlling dynamic adjustments of learning rate according to recent prediction errors, eta, was affected by our pharmacological manipulation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a result from model parameter comparison with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: Simulated agents with low to intermediate levels of eta achieved the best task performance.
source: The results revealed that simulated agents with low to intermediate levels of eta achieved the best task performance, with models equipped with the highest etas performing particularly poorly (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is a result from simulation analysis with reference to Figure 8D.

claim: Low baseline performers tended to have particularly high values of eta under the baseline condition.
source: It is noteworthy that low baseline performers tended to have particularly high values of eta under the baseline condition (low baseline performers: 0.33 (0.02) vs. high baseline performers: 0.25 (0.01); t(46) = 2.59, p = 0.01, d = 0.53), explaining why these individuals saw the largest improvements under the MA condition.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: MA alters performance by changing the degree to which learning rates are adjusted according to recent prediction errors (eta), in particular by reducing the strength of such adjustments in low baseline performers to push them closer to task-specific optimal values.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that MA alters performance by changing the degree to which learning rates are adjusted according to recent prediction errors (eta), in particular by reducing the strength of such adjustments in low baseline performers to push them closer to task-specific optimal values.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of the study.

claim: High baseline performers displayed higher overall inverse temperatures compared to low baseline performers.
source: When comparing other model parameters between low and high baseline performer across drug sessions, we found that high baseline performer displayed higher overall inverse temperatures (2.97 (0.05) vs. 2.11 (0.08); t(93) = 7.94, p < 0.001, d = 1.33).
evidence: This is a statistical result from model parameter comparison.

claim: MA specifically affects the eta parameter while leaving other parameters, such as the inverse temperature, unaffected.
source: This pattern of results suggests that MA specifically affects the eta parameter while leaving other parameters, such as the inverse temperature, unaffected.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model parameter results.

claim: The inability to make inference about stochasticity leads to misestimation of volatility, particularly for high outcome noise phases.
source: We found that the inability to make inference about stochasticity, leads to misestimation of volatility, particularly for high outcome noise phases (Figure 9A, B).
evidence: This is a result from exploratory simulation analysis with reference to Figure 9A, B.

claim: The lesioned model shows similar behavior to the low-performer group, with reduced accuracy in later learning stages for stimuli with high outcome noise.
source: The model shows similar behavior to our low-performer group, with reduced accuracy in later learnings stages for stimuli with high outcome noise (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is an observation from exploratory simulation analysis with reference to Figure 9D.

claim: When simulated data from the two models were fit to the study's model, increased eta parameter estimates were observed for the lesioned model.
source: Finally, when we fit simulated data from the two models to our model, we see increased eta parameter estimates for the lesioned model.
evidence: This is a result from exploratory simulation analysis.

claim: MA may reduce the oversensitivity to volatility in low performers.
source: Together, these results may hint toward an overinterpretation of stochasticity in low performer of our task and that MA has beneficial effects for those individuals as it reduced the oversensitivity to volatility.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the exploratory simulation results.

claim: MA affected the relative weighting of reward prediction errors.
source: A key finding of the current study is that MA affected the relative weighting of reward prediction errors.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the study.

claim: MA was associated with lower weighting of prediction errors (quantified by lower eta parameters under MA).
source: MA was associated with lower weighting of prediction errors (quantified by lower eta parameters under MA).
evidence: This is a result from model parameter comparison.

claim: MA may prolong the impact of phasic dopamine signals, which in turn facilitates better learning of the task structure and learning rate adjustments.
source: In terms of the neurobiological implementation of this effect, MA may prolong the impact of phasic dopamine signals, which in turn facilitates better learning of the task structure and learning rate adjustments (Cook et al., 2019; Marshall et al., 2016; Volkow et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: MA might improve meta-control of when to shield and when to shift beliefs in low baseline performers.
source: Our data suggest that MA might improve meta-control of when to shield and when to shift beliefs in low baseline performers.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: It is possible that MA's effect on learning rate adjustments is driven by its influence on the noradrenaline system.
source: Moreover, it is possible that MA's effect on learning rate adjustments is driven by its influence on the noradrenaline system.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism.

claim: Noradrenaline is important for change detection.
source: In particular, evidence from experimental studies, together with pharmacological manipulations and lesion studies of the noradrenergic system suggest that noradrenaline is important for change detection (Muller et al., 2019; Nassar et al., 2012; Preuschoff et al., 2011; Set et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The benefits of MA on performance depend on the baseline task performance.
source: Another key finding of the current study is that the benefits of MA on performance depend on the baseline task performance.
evidence: This is a summary of a main finding from the study.

claim: MA selectively improved performance in participants that performed poorly in the baseline session.
source: Specifically, we found that MA selectively improved performance in participants that performed poorly in the baseline session.
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis.

claim: MA did not bring performance of low baseline performers to the level of performance of high baseline performers.
source: It is important to note, that MA did not bring performance of low baseline performers to the level of performance of high baseline performers.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: High performers gained a good representation of the task structure during the orientation practice session.
source: We speculate that high performers gained a good representation of the task structure during the orientation practice session, taking specific features of the task into account (change point probabilities, noise in the reward probabilities).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: The data do not support an inverted-U-shaped effect of catecholaminergic action given that performance of high performers did not decrease with MA.
source: Intriguingly, the data do not support an inverted-U-shaped effect of catecholaminergic action (Durstewitz and Seamans, 2008; Goschke and Bolte, 2018) given that performance of high performers did not decrease with MA.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in relation to existing theory.

claim: The inclusion of an orientation session might be a good strategy to control for practice and drug order effects.
source: Thus, the inclusion of an orientation session might be a good strategy to control for practice and drug order effects.
evidence: This is a methodological conclusion drawn from the study design.

claim: Methylphenidate improved reversal learning performance to a greater degree in participants with higher dopamine synthesis capacity.
source: They demonstrated that methylphenidate improved reversal learning performance to a greater degree in participants with higher dopamine synthesis capacity, thus establishing the baseline dependency principle for methylphenidate.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Individual baseline differences strongly influence drug effects and thus should be considered in pharmacological studies.
source: However, our result that initial task performance strongly affected the effect of MA is in line with the pattern of results showing that individual baseline differences strongly influence drug effects and thus should be considered in pharmacological studies (Cools and D'Esposito, 2011; Durstewitz and Seamans, 2008; van den Bosch et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There is evidence that stimulants improve performance only in low performers.
source: Indeed, there is evidence from the broader literature on the effects of psychostimulants on cognitive performance, that suggest that stimulants improve performance only in low performers (Ilieva et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: MA and methylphenidate differ in their primary mechanisms of action.
source: First, MA and methylphenidate differ in their primary mechanisms of action: MPH acts mainly as a reuptake blocker, whereas MA increases synaptic levels of catecholamines by inhibiting the vesicular monoamine transporter 2 and inhibiting the enzyme monoamine oxidase.
evidence: This is a statement about the pharmacological properties of the drugs.

claim: The current data provide evidence that relative to PL, MA facilitates the ability to dynamically adjust learning from prediction errors.
source: The current data provide evidence that relative to PL, MA facilitates the ability to dynamically adjust learning from prediction errors.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the study.

claim: These results advance existing literature by presenting evidence for a causal link between catecholaminergic modulation and learning flexibility.
source: These results advance existing literature by presenting evidence for a causal link between catecholaminergic modulation and learning flexibility and further highlight a baseline dependency principle for catecholaminergic modulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the contribution of the study.
